claim: Fbxl7 encodes an F-box protein with 11 leucine-rich repeats (LRRs).
source: we identified mutant alleles of the Drosophila Fbxl7 gene (CG4221), which encodes a protein with an F-box and 11 leucine-rich repeats (LRRs) (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by the manuscript text describing the protein structure and by Figure 1A showing the protein domains.

claim: Fbxl7 has a conserved human ortholog (FBXL7) that shares 49% amino acid identity over the region spanning the F-box and the LRRs.
source: Fbxl7 has a conserved human ortholog (FBXL7) that shares 49% amino acid identity over the region spanning the F-box and the LRRs.
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by sequence comparison data.

claim: Most proteins with F-box and LRR motifs function as part of an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase.
source: Most proteins with these motifs function as part of an SCF-type ubiquitin ligase, a protein complex which polyubiquitylates substrate proteins and targets them for degradation by the proteasome (Skaar et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Skaar et al., 2013.

claim: Mutant clones of all three Fbxl7 alleles were overrepresented in the adult eye compared to clones of the parental FRT82B chromosome.
source: Mutant clones of all three alleles were overrepresented in the adult eye when compared to clones of the parental FRT82B chromosome (Figure 1B), suggesting that these Fbxl7 mutations cause increased tissue growth (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-E comparing mutant and control mosaic eyes.

claim: Fbxl7 mutations cause increased tissue growth.
source: Mutant clones of all three alleles were overrepresented in the adult eye when compared to clones of the parental FRT82B chromosome (Figure 1B), suggesting that these Fbxl7 mutations cause increased tissue growth (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: The claim is supported by mosaic eye data showing overrepresentation of mutant tissue.

claim: Two of the Fbxl7 mutations generate premature stop codons upstream of all conserved domains.
source: Two of the mutations generate premature stop codons upstream of all conserved domains, while the third causes a cysteine-to-tyrosine change in a conserved residue in one of the LRRs (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C)
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular characterization data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: The third Fbxl7 mutation causes a cysteine-to-tyrosine change in a conserved residue in one of the LRRs that likely interferes with the normal function of the protein.
source: while the third causes a cysteine-to-tyrosine change in a conserved residue in one of the LRRs (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C) that likely interferes with the normal function of the protein
evidence: The claim is supported by molecular data and inference about functional impact based on conservation.

claim: All three Fbxl7 alleles reduce or eliminate Fbxl7 function.
source: indicating that all three alleles reduce or eliminate Fbxl7 function.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the molecular nature of the mutations and their phenotypic effects.

claim: A Mi{MIC} minos insertion in the first intron of Fbxl7 results in a strong loss-of-function phenotype similar to other mutant alleles.
source: We also found that a Mi{MIC} minos insertion in the first intron of Fbxl7 (Venken et al., 2011) results in a strong loss-of-function phenotype similar to our other mutant alleles (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by phenotypic data shown in supplementary figures and citation to Venken et al., 2011.

claim: Flies homozygous for each of the Fbxl7 mutations are viable and fertile.
source: Although clones of mutant cells display a clear growth advantage, flies homozygous for each of these Fbxl7 mutations are viable and fertile.
evidence: The claim is directly stated based on observations of fly viability and fertility.

claim: The wings of Fbxl7 homozygotes or hemizygotes are larger and more rounded than wild-type wings.
source: However, the wings of Fbxl7 homozygotes or hemizygotes (Fbxl7-/Deficiency) are larger and more rounded than wild-type wings (Figure 1F–H; quantified in Figure 1L and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by wing morphology data shown in Figure 1F-H and quantified in Figure 1L.

claim: The distance between the cross veins is reduced in Fbxl7 mutant wings.
source: and the distance between the cross veins is reduced (Figure 1F–G, Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing morphology measurements shown in figures.

claim: The same alterations in wing area and spacing between the cross veins were observed when Fbxl7 function was reduced by RNAi.
source: The same alterations in wing area and spacing between the cross veins were also observed when Fbxl7 function was reduced by RNAi (Figure 1L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B) (Dui et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNAi knockdown data shown in figures and cited from Dui et al., 2012.

claim: The combination of overgrowth and reduced spacing of the cross veins is reminiscent of mutations in the Ft branch of the Hippo signaling pathway.
source: The combination of overgrowth and reduced spacing of the cross veins is especially reminiscent of mutations in the Ft branch of the Hippo signaling pathway (Bryant et al., 1988; Mahoney et al., 1991; Clark et al., 1995; Villano and Katz, 1995; Mao et al., 2006; Matakatsu and Blair, 2008; Mao et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published phenotypes of Ft pathway mutations.

claim: Fbxl7 mutant cells behave as supercompetitors similar to loss-of-function mutations in ft or in core components of the Hippo pathway such as hpo or wts.
source: Thus Fbxl7 mutant cells do indeed behave as supercompetitors similar to loss-of-function mutations in ft or in core components of the Hippo pathway such as hpo or wts (Tyler et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by cell competition assay data and comparison to published results from Tyler et al., 2007.

claim: Elevated levels of activated caspase-3 were observed especially in wild-type cells adjacent to Fbxl7 mutant clones.
source: We observed elevated levels of activated caspase-3, a marker of apoptosis, especially in wild-type cells adjacent to Fbxl7 mutant clones (Figure 1M–M″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1M-M″.

claim: In Fbxl7 mutant clones in the eye imaginal disc, expression of a diap1-GFP reporter gene was increased, especially posterior to the morphogenetic furrow.
source: In Fbxl7 mutant clones in the eye imaginal disc, expression of a diap1-GFP reporter gene (Zhang et al., 2008) was increased, especially posterior to the morphogenetic furrow (Figure 1N–N″)
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter gene expression data shown in Figure 1N-N″ and citation to Zhang et al., 2008.

claim: Increased diap1-GFP expression in Fbxl7 mutant clones is consistent with increased Yki activity.
source: In Fbxl7 mutant clones in the eye imaginal disc, expression of a diap1-GFP reporter gene (Zhang et al., 2008) was increased, especially posterior to the morphogenetic furrow (Figure 1N–N″) consistent with increased Yki activity.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the known relationship between diap1 expression and Yki activity.

claim: The enlarged wing phenotype observed upon expression of Fbxl7RNAi was enhanced by heterozygosity of the wtsX1 allele.
source: Additionally, the enlarged wing phenotype observed upon expression of Fbxl7RNAi was enhanced by heterozygosity of the wtsX1 allele (Figure 1—figure supplement 2K–L).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: Loss of Fbxl7 leads to increased growth via the Hippo pathway.
source: Together these results indicate that loss of Fbxl7 leads to increased growth via the Hippo pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including reporter gene expression and genetic interactions.

claim: Overexpressing Fbxl7 in the wing imaginal disc resulted in smaller adult wings with reduced distance between the cross veins.
source: When we overexpressed Fbxl7 in the wing imaginal disc, the adult wings were smaller and had a reduced distance between the cross veins (Figure 1I–L, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The claim is supported by wing morphology data from overexpression experiments shown in figures.

claim: Overexpressing Fbxl7 reduced the length of distal leg segments.
source: Overexpressing Fbxl7 also reduced the length of distal leg segments (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The claim is supported by leg morphology data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The reduction in wing size from Fbxl7 overexpression was suppressed by heterozygosity of the wtsX1 allele.
source: This reduction in wing size was suppressed by heterozygosity of the wtsX1 allele (Figure 1P–R, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic interaction data shown in figures.

claim: Overexpression of Fbxl7C616Y, if at all, caused a slight increase in wing size.
source: When we overexpressed a form of Fbxl7 bearing the missense mutation identified in the screen, Fbxl7C616Y, there was, if at all, a slight increase in wing size (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by wing size measurements shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The Fbxl7C616Y mutation disrupts the normal function of the protein and likely functions as a dominant-negative mutation under conditions of overexpression.
source: suggesting that this mutation disrupts the normal function of the protein and likely functions as a dominant-negative mutation at least under conditions of overexpression.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotypic effects of overexpressing the mutant protein.

claim: Overexpression of Fbxl7 reduced expression of an ex-lacZ reporter in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Overexpression of Fbxl7 reduced expression of an ex-lacZ reporter (Boedigheimer and Laughon, 1993; Hamaratoglu et al., 2006) in a cell-autonomous manner (Figure 1O–O′).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter gene expression data shown in Figure 1O-O′ and citations.

claim: Wild-type cells close to Fbxl7-overexpressing cells had increased ex-lacZ reporter expression, especially in the notum of the wing disc and in the eye disc.
source: However, wild-type cells close to the Fbxl7-overexpressing cells had increased ex-lacZ reporter expression, especially in the notum of the wing disc and in the eye disc (Figure 1—figure supplement 2M–N′).
evidence: The claim is supported by reporter gene expression data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A similar non-autonomous increase in Yki activity was observed with the bantam sensor.
source: A similar phenomenon was observed with the bantam sensor (Figure 1—figure supplement 2O–O′) (Brennecke et al., 2003), which is expressed at higher levels when Yki activity is reduced.
evidence: The claim is supported by bantam sensor data shown in supplementary figures and citation to Brennecke et al., 2003.

claim: This non-autonomous increase in Yki activity is similar to that seen when Ft is overexpressed or at boundaries of differential Ds or Fj activity.
source: This non-autonomous increase in Yki activity is similar to that seen when Ft is overexpressed (Matakatsu and Blair, 2012) or at boundaries of differential Ds or Fj activity (Willecke et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison to published observations from Matakatsu and Blair, 2012 and Willecke et al., 2008.

claim: Fbxl7 functions as a negative regulator of growth via the Hippo pathway.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Fbxl7 functions as a negative regulator of growth via the Hippo pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including loss-of-function and gain-of-function phenotypes and reporter gene expression.

claim: The multiple phenotypic similarities between alterations in Ft levels and Fbxl7 levels suggest that Fbxl7 functions in proximity to Ft.
source: Moreover, the multiple phenotypic similarities between alterations in Ft levels and Fbxl7 levels suggest that Fbxl7 functions in proximity to Ft.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the phenotypic similarities between Ft and Fbxl7 manipulations.

claim: A polyclonal antibody to an N-terminal portion of Fbxl7 detects uniform Fbxl7 expression throughout the wing imaginal disc.
source: A polyclonal antibody to an N-terminal portion of Fbxl7 detects uniform Fbxl7 expression throughout the wing imaginal disc (Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Fbxl7 expression is slightly enriched at the dorsal-ventral boundary in the wing pouch.
source: with a slight enrichment at the dorsal-ventral boundary in the pouch as is also observed for Ft protein (Mao et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data and comparison to published Ft localization from Mao et al., 2009.

claim: At the cellular level, punctate Fbxl7 staining is observed outlining the apical profiles of cells.
source: At the cellular level, punctate staining is observed outlining the apical profiles of cells
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: Apical Fbxl7 staining is absent in homozygous mutant clones of the Fbxl7Q201X allele.
source: which is absent in homozygous mutant clones of the Fbxl7Q201X allele (Figure 2B–B′) indicating that the truncated protein generated by this allele is likely unstable.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in mutant clones shown in Figure 2B-B′.

claim: The truncated protein generated by the Fbxl7Q201X allele is likely unstable.
source: which is absent in homozygous mutant clones of the Fbxl7Q201X allele (Figure 2B–B′) indicating that the truncated protein generated by this allele is likely unstable.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the absence of protein staining in mutant clones.

claim: In Fbxl7C616Y clones, apical puncta are absent but cytoplasmic staining is observed above background levels.
source: In Fbxl7C616Y clones, apical puncta are absent but cytoplasmic staining is observed above background levels, indicating that the mutant protein is present but does not localize apically (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: The Fbxl7C616Y mutant protein is present but does not localize apically.
source: In Fbxl7C616Y clones, apical puncta are absent but cytoplasmic staining is observed above background levels, indicating that the mutant protein is present but does not localize apically (not shown).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the pattern of protein staining in mutant clones.

claim: FLAG-Fbxl7 exhibits an apical localization that is very similar to that of the endogenous protein.
source: An Fbxl7 protein with an N-terminal FLAG epitope tag (FLAG-Fbxl7) exhibits an apical localization that is very similar to that of the endogenous protein (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data comparing endogenous and tagged protein shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: Fbxl7 localizes to the subapical region of cells, apical to the adherens junctions marked by E-cadherin.
source: Using either the anti-Fbxl7 antibody (Figure 2C,E) or FLAG-Fbxl7 (Figure 2D,F), we found that Fbxl7 localizes to the subapical region of cells, apical to the adherens junctions marked by E-cadherin.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data with E-cadherin shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: FLAG-Fbxl7 is also found in intracellular puncta.
source: FLAG-Fbxl7 is also found in intracellular puncta (Figure 2G).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: FLAG-Fbxl7 protein bearing the C616Y missense mutation displays only diffuse cytoplasmic localization.
source: In contrast, FLAG-Fbxl7 protein bearing the C616Y missense mutation displays only diffuse cytoplasmic localization (Figure 2H)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The normal function of Fbxl7 may be contingent upon its localization to the apical region or cytoplasmic puncta.
source: suggesting that the normal function of Fbxl7 may be contingent upon its localization to the apical region or cytoplasmic puncta.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the mislocalization of the non-functional C616Y mutant protein.

claim: In the peripodial epithelium, confocal sections show Fbxl7 puncta with diameters typically in the range of 400–500 nm (some as large as 1000 nm) with a hollow interior.
source: In Drosophila S2 cells (not shown) or the flattened cells of the peripodial epithelium (Figure 2I), confocal sections show puncta with diameters typically in the range of 400–500 nm (some as large as 1000 nm) with a hollow interior
evidence: The claim is supported by microscopy measurements shown in Figure 2I.

claim: The hollow interior of Fbxl7 puncta is consistent with the possibility that these might be vesicles.
source: confocal sections show puncta with diameters typically in the range of 400–500 nm (some as large as 1000 nm) with a hollow interior, consistent with the possibility that these might be vesicles.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the morphology of the puncta.

claim: In the dorsal part of the wing pouch, FLAG-Fbxl7 localizes preferentially to the proximal side of cells.
source: In the dorsal part of the wing pouch, where polarization of D is most evident (Brittle et al., 2012), FLAG-Fbxl7 localizes preferentially to the proximal side of cells (Figure 2J,K–K‴).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2J,K-K‴ and citation to Brittle et al., 2012.

claim: Both anti-Fbxl7 and anti-Ft revealed apical staining in a punctate manner with a considerable degree of overlap.
source: Both anti-Fbxl7 and anti-Ft revealed apical staining in a punctate manner with a considerable degree of overlap (Figure 3A–A″).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3A-A″.

claim: FLAG-Fbxl7 and Ft co-localize at the apical membrane.
source: Additionally, we observed co-localization of FLAG-Fbxl7 and Ft at the apical membrane (Figure 3B–B″)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 3B-B″.

claim: FLAG-Fbxl7 and Ft co-localize in cytoplasmic puncta, many of which were basally located.
source: as well as in cytoplasmic puncta (Figure 3B″–B‴, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), many of which were basally located.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in figures.

claim: FatICD co-immunoprecipitates with FLAG-Fbxl7 in S2 cells.
source: FatICD co-immunoprecipitates with FLAG-Fbxl7, whereas association of FatICD with FLAG-Fbxl7C616Y is greatly reduced (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Association of FatICD with FLAG-Fbxl7C616Y is greatly reduced compared to wild-type Fbxl7.
source: FatICD co-immunoprecipitates with FLAG-Fbxl7, whereas association of FatICD with FLAG-Fbxl7C616Y is greatly reduced (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fbxl7 interacts with Ft mostly via its LRRs.
source: We also examined the ability of truncated Fbxl7 proteins to interact with Ft and find that Fbxl7 interacts with Ft mostly via its LRRs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data with truncated proteins shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A weaker interaction is observed between Ft and the N-terminal portion of Fbxl7.
source: A weaker interaction is also observed between Ft and the N-terminal portion of Fbxl7.
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Wild-type Fbxl7 can associate, either directly or indirectly, with the intracellular domain of Ft.
source: Thus wild-type Fbxl7 can associate, either directly or indirectly, with the intracellular domain of Ft and this interaction mostly occurs via the LRRs of Fbxl7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: The apical localization of Fbxl7 was absent in ft clones.
source: The apical localization of Fbxl7 was absent in ft clones (Figure 3D–D‴).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in ft mutant clones shown in Figure 3D-D‴.

claim: An increase in diffuse cytoplasmic Fbxl7 staining was observed in ft clones.
source: However, an increase in diffuse cytoplasmic staining was observed (Figure 3E–E‴).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E-E‴.

claim: The localization of Fbxl7 to the apical region is dependent upon Ft.
source: Thus the localization of Fbxl7 to the apical region is dependent upon Ft and in the absence of Ft, Fbxl7 re-localizes to the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the loss of apical Fbxl7 in ft mutant clones.

claim: In the absence of Ft, Fbxl7 re-localizes to the cytoplasm.
source: Thus the localization of Fbxl7 to the apical region is dependent upon Ft and in the absence of Ft, Fbxl7 re-localizes to the cytoplasm.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the redistribution of Fbxl7 in ft mutant clones.

claim: Punctate localization of FLAG-Fbxl7 was still observed in ft clones.
source: Surprisingly, unlike the apical localization, punctate localization of FLAG-Fbxl7 was still observed in ft clones indicating that the localization of Fbxl7 in these cytoplasmic puncta is independent of Ft (Figure 3F–F″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in ft mutant clones shown in Figure 3F-F″.

claim: The localization of Fbxl7 in cytoplasmic puncta is independent of Ft.
source: Surprisingly, unlike the apical localization, punctate localization of FLAG-Fbxl7 was still observed in ft clones indicating that the localization of Fbxl7 in these cytoplasmic puncta is independent of Ft (Figure 3F–F″).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the persistence of punctate Fbxl7 in ft mutant clones.

claim: Increasing Fbxl7 levels resulted in clearly increased levels of apical Ft.
source: Increasing Fbxl7 levels resulted in clearly increased levels of apical Ft (Figure 3G–G′)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Fbxl7 overexpression clones shown in Figure 3G-G′.

claim: Increasing Fbxl7 levels resulted in slightly increased cytoplasmic staining of Ft.
source: and slightly increased cytoplasmic staining of Ft (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: A slight elevation of apical Ft levels was observed in Fbxl7 mutant clones.
source: Surprisingly, a slight elevation of apical Ft levels was also observed in Fbxl7 mutant clones (Figure 3H–H″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Fbxl7 mutant clones shown in Figure 3H-H″.

claim: The overall levels of Ft protein in imaginal discs were not obviously changed by altering Fbxl7 levels.
source: The overall levels of Ft protein in imaginal discs, as assessed by Western blotting, were not obviously changed in either case (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: These results are inconsistent with Fbxl7 promoting Ft degradation.
source: These results are inconsistent with Fbxl7 promoting Ft degradation and instead suggest that Fbxl7 regulates Ft localization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of change in total Ft protein levels.

claim: Fbxl7 regulates Ft localization.
source: These results are inconsistent with Fbxl7 promoting Ft degradation and instead suggest that Fbxl7 regulates Ft localization.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the effects of Fbxl7 on apical Ft levels without changing total levels.

claim: An obvious increase in Ft ubiquitylation from expressing Fbxl7 in S2 cells was not observed.
source: In support of this, we do not observe an obvious increase in Ft ubiquitylation from expressing Fbxl7 in S2 cells (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by ubiquitylation assay data.

claim: In ds mutant clones, apical localization of Fbxl7 is no longer observed as discrete puncta at cell edges but is rather more diffuse.
source: In ds mutant clones, apical localization of Fbxl7 is no longer observed as discrete puncta at cell edges but is rather more diffuse (Figure 4A–A″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in ds mutant clones shown in Figure 4A-A″.

claim: In ds clones, Fbxl7 is still predominantly at an apical location.
source: Moreover, in contrast to ft clones, we do not see an increase in cytoplasmic Fbxl7 in ds clones at more basal focal planes, indicating that Fbxl7 is still predominantly at an apical location (Figure 4B–B″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in ds mutant clones shown in Figure 4B-B″.

claim: Changes in Fbxl7 localization in ds clones could be a consequence of the more diffuse localization of Ft in ds clones.
source: These changes in Fbxl7 localization could simply be a consequence of the more diffuse localization of Ft that is observed in ds clones (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Ma et al., 2003; Mao et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is inferred from published observations of Ft localization in ds mutants.

claim: Fj is required for normal localization of Ds and Ft.
source: Fj is required for normal localization of Ds and Ft (Strutt and Strutt, 2002; Ma et al., 2003).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strutt and Strutt, 2002 and Ma et al., 2003.

claim: Subtle effects on Fbxl7 localization are seen in fj clones, similar to those seen in ds clones.
source: In agreement with this, we see subtle effects on Fbxl7 localization in fj clones, which appears similar to that seen in ds clones (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in fj mutant clones shown in supplementary figures.

claim: When Fbxl7 is overexpressed in clones, cells have more prominent apical expression of Ds in puncta.
source: When Fbxl7 is overexpressed in clones, cells have more prominent apical expression of Ds in puncta (Figure 4C–C″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Fbxl7 overexpression clones shown in Figure 4C-C″.

claim: In wild-type cells bordering Fbxl7-overexpressing clones, Ds staining is reduced and accumulates in prominent puncta at the surface that abuts the Fbxl7-overexpressing cells.
source: Additionally, in wild-type cells bordering the Fbxl7-overexpressing clone, Ds staining is reduced and accumulates in prominent puncta at the surface that abuts the Fbxl7-overexpressing cells (Figure 4D–E″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D-E″.

claim: Ds may be drawn toward Fbxl7-overexpressing cells due to the increased Ft levels.
source: Given that Ds can be drawn toward cells with greater levels of Ft (Ma et al., 2003), Ds may be drawn toward Fbxl7-overexpressing cells due to the increased Ft levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from published observations and the increased Ft levels in Fbxl7-overexpressing cells.

claim: The puncta of Ds in adjacent wild-type cells are in register with Fbxl7 puncta.
source: Furthermore, the puncta of Ds in adjacent wild-type cells are in register with Fbxl7 puncta, consistent with the coupling of Ds in wild-type cells to Fbxl7-bound Ft within the clone.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining observations.

claim: The alignment of Ds puncta with Fbxl7 puncta is consistent with the coupling of Ds in wild-type cells to Fbxl7-bound Ft within the clone.
source: Furthermore, the puncta of Ds in adjacent wild-type cells are in register with Fbxl7 puncta, consistent with the coupling of Ds in wild-type cells to Fbxl7-bound Ft within the clone.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the spatial relationship between Ds and Fbxl7 puncta.

claim: In Fbxl7 mutant clones, there is, at best, a very slight elevation of Ds levels.
source: In Fbxl7 mutant clones, there is, at best, a very slight elevation of Ds levels (Figure 4F–F″).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in Fbxl7 mutant clones shown in Figure 4F-F″.

claim: The effects of Fbxl7 on Ds levels are minor compared to the effects on Ft levels.
source: Thus, the effects of Fbxl7 on Ds levels are minor compared to the effects on Ft levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from comparing the effects of Fbxl7 on Ds versus Ft.

claim: Ds was not detected in immunoprecipitates of Fbxl7 when the two proteins were co-expressed in S2 cells.
source: Additionally, we could not detect Ds in immunoprecipitates of Fbxl7 when the two proteins were co-expressed in S2 cells (not shown).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: Fbxl7 binds to and functions with Ft rather than Ds.
source: Together, these findings suggest that Fbxl7 binds to and functions with Ft rather than Ds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of direct interaction between Fbxl7 and Ds and the minor effects on Ds levels.

claim: Fbxl7 and Ds co-localize at apical membranes and in more basally located cytoplasmic puncta.
source: Despite this, we did observe co-localization of Fbxl7 and Ds at apical membranes and in more basally located cytoplasmic puncta (Figure 4G–G″).
evidence: The claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4G-G″.

claim: The co-localization of Fbxl7 and Ds at the cell surface may result from Fbxl7 bound to Ft that is in turn bound to Ds.
source: In the absence of evidence for direct interactions between Fbxl7 and Ds, their co-localization, at least at the cell surface, may result from Fbxl7 bound to Ft that is in turn bound to Ds.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the lack of direct Fbxl7-Ds interaction and the known Ft-Ds interaction.

claim: Ds binding to Ft induces the phosphorylation of the ICD of Ft, which requires the protein kinase Dco.
source: Ds binding to Ft induces the phosphorylation of the ICD of Ft, which requires the protein kinase, Dco (Feng and Irvine, 2009; Sopko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Feng and Irvine, 2009 and Sopko et al., 2009.

claim: The apical localization of Fbxl7 was not obviously changed in clones of the dco3 allele that is unable to phosphorylate Ft.
source: The apical localization of Fbxl7 was not obviously changed in clones of the dco3 allele that is unable to phosphorylate Ft (Figure 4H–H″) (Sopko et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in dco3 mutant clones shown in Figure 4H-H″ and citation to Sopko et al., 2009.

claim: Dco is capable of binding to Fbxl7 as assessed by co-immunoprecipitation from S2 cells.
source: While Dco is capable of binding to Fbxl7 as assessed by co-immunoprecipitation from S2 cells (Figure 4J)
evidence: The claim is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The apical localization of Fbxl7 was still observed in clones of the null dco allele, dcole88.
source: the apical localization of Fbxl7 was still observed in clones of the null dco allele, dcole88 (Figure 4I–I″)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunostaining data in dcole88 mutant clones shown in Figure 4I-I″.

claim: Dco function is unnecessary for the apical localization of Fbxl7.
source: thus indicating that Dco function is altogether unnecessary for the apical localization of Fbxl7.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the normal Fbxl7 localization in dco null mutant clones.

claim: Changes in Hippo signaling do not regulate Fbxl7 levels or localization.
source: Furthermore, while changes in Fbxl7 alter Hippo signaling, changes in Hippo signaling do not regulate Fbxl7 levels or localization, as Fbxl7 localization is normal in clones mutant for dachs or wts (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C″).
